s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a small island south of Crete
to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
s.c: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

s.d: (derivative of {L:κλάω<SDBG:κλάω:000000>} ‘to break,’ {D:19.34}) a fragment or piece resulting from the action of breaking

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian woman who sent greetings in {S:05500402100026}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus (compare {D:93.359}), a Roman emperor, who ruled from 41 A.D. to 54 A.D.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer in Jerusalem

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
s.g: to weep; to wail; to lament; weeping; crying

s.d: to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
s.c: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
s.g: to eat a meal; to have a meal
s.c: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ ⟦Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7⟧. No doubt the reference in ⟦Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7⟧ is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See LN 23.28.

s.d: an instrument used for locking and unlocking doors and gates
s.c: In rendering ⟦Revelation 9:1|Revelation 9:1⟧ it may not be possible to speak of ‘the key to the abyss,’ but rather ‘the key to the entrance to the abyss’ or ‘the key used in opening or closing the gate to the abyss.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Take, Obtain, Gain, Lose
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κλείς<SDBG:κλείς:000000>}[a] ‘key,’ {D:6.220}) a means of acquiring something
s.g: the means of; the key to
s.c: One may also translate this expression in ⟦Luke 11:52|Luke 11:52⟧ as ‘you have kept to yourselves the key to knowledge’ or ‘… the means by which one may gain understanding.’

s.d: to cause something to be shut
s.g: to shut; to make shut; to close
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of this expression in ⟦Acts 5:23|Acts 5:23⟧ would be ‘we found the jail securely locked.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to close the bowels) to refuse to show compassion
s.g: to not have compassion for; to close one’s heart toward

s.d: to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a believer whom Jesus met on the road to Emmaus

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: a good reputation as an index of status
(derivative of {L:κλέπτω<SDBG:κλέπτω:000000>} ‘to steal,’ {D:57.232}) a person who steals
to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
a more or less tender, flexible branch, as of a vine

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a member of the church at Philippi
to receive something of considerable value which has not been earned
s.g: to receive; to be given; to gain possession of

s.d: to receive a possession or benefit as a gift from someone who has died, generally a parent
s.g: to inherit; to receive from a deceased parent
s.c: In some languages the process of inheritance must be made rather explicit, so that ‘he will inherit the property’ must be expressed as ‘he will become owner of the property which his father said he should have.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000000>}[a] ‘to gain as a possession,’ {D:57.131}) a valuable possession which has been received
(derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000001>}[b] ‘to inherit,’ {D:57.138}) that which is received from a deceased person
s.c: In ⟦Luke 12:13|Luke 12:13⟧ it may also be possible to render κληρονομία as ‘the property our father left us’ or ‘the property which our father said should be given to us.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000000>}[a] ‘to gain as a possession,’ {D:57.131}) one who receives something as a gift
s.g: one who receives; one who comes into possession of; receiver; heir

s.d: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000001>}[b] ‘to inherit,’ {D:57.138}) the person who inherits possessions
a specially marked pebble, piece of pottery, or stick employed in making decisions based upon chance
s.c: Both in form as well as in function, the closest equivalent of κλῆρος is frequently a term which refers to dice. In ⟦Luke 23:34|Luke 23:34⟧ a term for dice would be particularly appropriate.|It is not possible to know the particular method employed in ‘choosing by lot,’ for evidently various devices were used. In ⟦Acts 1:26|Acts 1:26⟧ (ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτοῖς ‘they drew lots,’ literally ‘they gave them lots’), it is probable that small sticks were handed out. See also footnote under κληρόω.

s.d: that which is given as a rightful possession (often in the sense of an inheritance)

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: a responsibility, function, or ministry which has been assigned to a person
s.c: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in ⟦Acts 1:17|Acts 1:17⟧, see LN 63.18.

s.dp: Help, Care For › Entrust To the Care Of
s.d: what has been assigned as someone’s responsibility to take care of
a share or portion which has been assigned or granted
s.c: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in ⟦Acts 1:17|Acts 1:17⟧, see LN 37.101.

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the lot falls upon someone) the process of choosing, with the probable implication of discerning God’s will in this manner
s.g: to choose by lot; to select by lot
s.c: In some societies the closest natural equivalents of deciding by lot are procedures involving ‘drawing straws’ or ‘throwing dice’ or ‘throwing down sticks’ or ‘dropping pebbles.’

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of κληρόω ‘to be chosen by lot,’ not occurring in the NT) to choose, with the implication of supernatural or divine intervention or guidance{N:001}
s.g: to choose in accordance with the will of God

s.d: to urgently invite someone to accept responsibilities for a particular task, implying a new relationship to the one who does the calling
s.g: to call; to call to a task
s.c: It is rare that one can translate καλέω, κλῆσις, and προσκαλέω as simply ‘to call’ in the sense of ‘to speak to someone at a distance and tell them to come.’ For example, in ⟦2 Thessalonians 2:14|2 Thessalonians 2:14⟧ it may be necessary to render the above clause as ‘through the good news we preached, which summoned you to do this.’ Similarly, in ⟦Acts 16:10|Acts 16:10⟧ one may translate ‘because God has urgently invited us to preach the good news to the people there.’

s.d: the state of having been called to a particular task and/or relation
s.c: As in the case of καλέω, κλῆσις, and προσκαλέω (LN 33.312), it may be entirely impossible to use a term in a receptor language which means literally ‘to call.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to translate ⟦Ephesians 4:1|Ephesians 4:1⟧ as ‘I ask you then … live worthy of the responsibility which God has urgently invited you to accept’ or ‘… live worthy of the task which God has given you to do.’

s.d: the station in life or social role which one has
s.c: In this context, κλῆσις refers to the status or role of being either a slave or a free person. In a number of languages this expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:20|1 Corinthians 7:20⟧ can be best translated as ‘everyone should continue to be the same kind of person that he was when he was called.’ Such an expression must, of course, refer to one’s position in society and in the total social structure, not to particular aspects of moral or immoral behavior.

s.d: pertaining to having been called
s.c: As in the case of the translation of meanings in LN 33.312 and LN 33.313, it may be necessary likewise to make certain semantic adjustments in the translation of κλητός . For example, the phrase in ⟦Romans 1:1|Romans 1:1⟧ may be rendered as ‘urgently invited to be an apostle’ or even ‘summoned and commissioned to be an apostle.’

s.d: pertaining to having been invited
s.c: It is possible that this expression in ⟦Matthew 22:14|Matthew 22:14⟧ was a common popular saying, namely, an adage. There are certain problems in the understanding of this adage in ⟦Matthew 22:14|Matthew 22:14⟧, for it would seem as though many persons are invited to do something, but few are permitted to do it. Perhaps this should be understood in the sense of ‘many are invited to apply, but few are selected.’ In this context, of course, both the invitation and the selection would be by God.

s.d: a dome-like structure made of clay, in which wood and dried grass were burned, and then after being heated, was used for baking bread
s.c: The function of κλίβανος may be described as ‘a place heated for baking bread,’ and it may be useful in some instances to employ a more extensive description of a κλίβανος in a glossary, but this is rarely necessary since function is far more important than form.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Sociopolitical Areas
s.d: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:001}
s.g: region; territory; land; district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
s.c: The meanings of γῆ, χώρα, κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

s.d: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
s.c: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

s.d: any piece of furniture employed for reclining or lying on
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 9:2|Matthew 9:2⟧ a rendering such as ‘stretcher’ or ‘cot’ is certainly more advisable than the traditional rendering ‘bed,’ which might imply a large piece of furniture. In each passage one must employ a term which is most likely to identify the type of object which fits the context.

s.d: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
s.c: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

s.d: to cause something to incline
s.g: to bow down (the head); to incline
s.c: See also LN 23.83.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to cause to flee or run away from
s.g: to cause to run away; to put to flight; to rout

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
s.g: to draw near; to draw to a close
s.c: For another interpretation of κλίνω in ⟦Luke 9:12|Luke 9:12⟧, see LN 68.51.

s.d: to begin to come to an end, with particular reference to the period of a day (a figurative meaning dependent upon the position of the sun)
s.c: For another interpretation of κλίνω in ⟦Luke 9:12|Luke 9:12⟧, see LN 67.118.

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to incline the face to the ground) to prostrate oneself before someone as an act of reverence, fear, or supplication

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Tire, Rest
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
s.g: to lie down to rest; to lie down to sleep
s.c: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’ ⟦Matthew 8:20|Matthew 8:20⟧, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In ⟦John 19:30|John 19:30⟧ this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see LN 16.16).

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: a group of persons engaged in eating together
s.c: Note that Luke employs κλισίας in essentially the same type of context in which Mark uses συμπόσια.

s.d: to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: a moving ridge or succession of swells on the surface of a body of water
to be tossed back and forth by the motion of waves
s.g: to be tossed about by waves
s.c: The imagery in ⟦Ephesians 4:14|Ephesians 4:14⟧ is based upon a person in a boat being tossed about by the waves. It may, therefore, be necessary to introduce a boat or ship in the context.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the husband of Μαρία 5, one of the women at the crucifixion

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to itch with respect to hearing) to have one’s ears tickled by what is heard{N:001}
s.g: to have itching ears; to desire to hear what one wants to hear; to be desirous of hearing

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a peninsula on the southwest coast of Asia Minor
a Roman copper coin worth 1/4 of an assarion ({S:04001002900008}) or 1/64 of a denarius ({S:04202002400006})
s.c: See LN 6.79.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the entire digestive apparatus, including stomach and intestines

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the uterus
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοιλία<SDBG:κοιλία:000000>}[a] ‘belly,’ {D:8.67}) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling{N:001}
s.c: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον, κοιλία, and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

s.d: desire for gratification of the body
s.g: physical desires; desires of the body
s.c: It is also possible that κοιλία in ⟦Romans 16:18|Romans 16:18⟧ refers to Jewish dietary laws and regulations.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
s.g: to be pregnant with; to carry in the womb
s.c: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render ⟦Luke 11:27|Luke 11:27⟧ as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: the state of being asleep
s.g: to sleep; to be asleep; sleep
s.c: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοιμάομαι<SDBG:κοιμάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to sleep,’ {D:23.66}) to sleep, as a euphemistic expression for the state of being dead
s.g: to be dead; to have died
s.c: Some translators have attempted to preserve the figure of speech in καθεύδω and κοιμάομαι by translating ‘to sleep’ rather than ‘to have died’ or ‘to be dead.’ Such a practice, however, has resulted in misunderstanding in a number of instances and has sometimes led to the doctrine of so-called ‘soul-sleep.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: the state of being asleep
s.g: to sleep; to be asleep; sleep
s.c: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’|In ⟦John 11:13|John 11:13⟧ κοίμησις is combined with ὕπνος apparently to stress the fact that the sleep was an ordinary or natural sleep.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: pertaining to sharing with someone else in a possession or a relationship implying mutual interest
s.c: Since the emphasis in ⟦Titus 1:4|Titus 1:4⟧ is upon the fact that Paul and Titus have the same faith, one may also translate as ‘… the faith that you and I have’ or ‘… the faith we both believe in.’

s.d: pertaining to being ritually unacceptable, either as the result of defilement or because of the very nature of the object itself (for example, ritually unacceptable animals)
s.c: It is possible that there is some subtle distinction in meaning, particularly on a connotative level, between κοινός and ἀκάθαρτος in ⟦Acts 10:14|Acts 10:14⟧, but it is difficult to determine the precise differences of meaning on the basis of existing contexts. The two terms are probably used in ⟦Acts 10:14|Acts 10:14⟧ primarily for the sake of emphasis.

s.d: pertaining to being of little value, in view of being ordinary and common
pertaining to being in common between two or more persons
s.c: It is also possible to understand κοινός in ⟦Jude 1:3|Jude 1:3⟧ as κοινός ‘shared, mutual’ (see LN 57.9).

s.d: to cause something to become unclean, profane, or ritually unacceptable{N:001}
s.g: to make unclean; to defile; to profane
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to translate literally the concept of unclean, for physical cleanliness and ritual acceptability are completely unrelated. In some languages it is necessary to translate κοινόω or βεβηλόω as to take away its holiness or to make something unacceptable to God. In many cultures one must express this concept as involving so-called negative taboo.

s.d: to call or to regard something as common or defiled
s.g: to call something common; to regard something as defiled

s.d: to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
to join with others in some activity
s.g: to join in doing; to share in doing

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to share blood and flesh) to have the characteristics and nature of a human being
s.g: to be a person; to be a physical being

s.d: an association involving close mutual relations and involvement
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
(derivative of {L:κοινωνέω<SDBG:κοινωνέω:000000>}[a] ‘to share,’ {D:57.98}) that which is readily shared
(derivative of {L:κοινωνέω<SDBG:κοινωνέω:000000>}[a] ‘to share,’ {D:57.98}) pertaining to willing and ready sharing
one who participates with another in some enterprise or matter of joint concern{N:001}
s.g: partner; associate; one who joins in with

s.d: a piece of furniture used for sleeping
s.c: It is not necessary to understand ⟦Luke 11:7|Luke 11:7⟧ to mean that the children were in the same bed with the man, but it is, of course, possible that the reference here is to a relatively humble house in which all the members of the family would sleep on a single raised platform. See also LN 10.37.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sexual Relations
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοίτη<SDBG:κοίτη:000000>}[a] ‘bed,’ {D:6.108}) to have sexual relations
s.g: sexual activity; sexual life; marriage relations
s.c: In some languages one may speak of ‘sexual life’ as ‘the way one lives with one’s wife’ or ‘how one treats one’s wife.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sexual Misbehavior
s.d: to engage in immoral sexual excess{N:001}

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to have bed, though in combination with ἔχω, κοίτη early acquired the metonymic meaning of sexual relations) to be in a state of pregnancy
s.c: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω, LN 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room in a house for sleeping
s.c: It would be wrong to render the expression ‘who was in charge of the king’s bedroom’ in ⟦Acts 12:20|Acts 12:20⟧ as meaning simply one who kept the bedroom clean. A person such as Blastus would have been a highly respected person with considerable responsibility for the king’s living quarters and personal affairs. The expression may be adequately rendered in ⟦Acts 12:20|Acts 12:20⟧ by speaking of Blastus as ‘a high official.’

s.d: a dye obtained from egg-clusters of a cochineal, collected from the leaves of Quercus coccifera
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 27:28|Matthew 27:28⟧ ‘scarlet robe’ may have implied high military rank.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
s.c: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

s.d: to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
s.c: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

s.d: praise as a means of gratifying someone’s vanity
to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
s.c: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

s.d: to strike or beat with the fist, either once or repeatedly
s.g: to strike with the fist; to beat with the fist

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κολαφίζω<SDBG:κολαφίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to beat with the fist,’ {D:19.7}) to cause injury or weakness or possibly a circumstantial difficulty
s.c: Though differences of interpretation exist concerning the meaning of ‘a thorn in my flesh’ (⟦2 Corinthians 12:7|2 Corinthians 12:7⟧), especially since some scholars have felt that this must refer to some kind of physical disability, it seems more likely to assume that it refers to some special personal circumstance such as the opposition Paul encountered in preaching the gospel, a reference suggested by ⟦2 Corinthians 12:10|2 Corinthians 12:10⟧ (see also LN 22.20).|Without some clear understanding of the reference of ‘a thorn in my flesh,’ it is difficult to determine precisely how κολαφίζω is to be interpreted in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:7|2 Corinthians 12:7⟧.

s.d: to begin an association with someone, whether temporary or permanent{N:001}
s.g: to join; to join oneself to; to become a part of
s.c: Though the Greek text of ⟦Acts 8:29|Acts 8:29⟧ says literally ‘join this carriage,’ in reality, of course, the association is not directly with the carriage, but with the man riding in the carriage. It is therefore necessary in a number of languages to translate κολλήθητι τῷ ἅρματι τούτῳ as ‘join the man riding in this carriage.’

s.d: to stick or cling to something
s.g: to cling to; to stick to

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to cling to heaven) to increase enormously the number of something, with the implication of reaching the attention of God
s.g: to increase greatly; to reach to high heaven

s.d: an ointment for the eyes
s.c: κολλούριον may often be rendered simply as ‘a medicine for the eyes.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Earn, Gain, Do Business
s.d: one who exchanges currency, either in terms of different types of currency or different values of the same currency
to cause something to be reduced in number or extent
s.g: to shorten; to decrease; to reduce in number
s.c: There may be difficulties involved in a strictly literal rendering of ‘those days will be shortened,’ for it might appear that each day would become shorter rather than that the number of days would be decreased. Therefore, one must render this expression in ⟦Matthew 24:22|Matthew 24:22⟧ in a number of languages as ‘those days will be fewer.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the region of the body extending from the breast to the legs, especially when a person is in a seated position
s.c: The term κόλπος occurs in several idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, the expression ‘who was in the bosom of the Father’ in ⟦John 1:18|John 1:18⟧ denotes an association of intimacy and affection (see LN 34.18). In a context referring to the position of a person at a meal (as in ⟦John 13:23|John 13:23⟧), κόλπος indicates an honored place (see LN 17.25). In ⟦Luke 16:22|Luke 16:22⟧ κόλπος Ἀβραάμ signifies the heavenly abode (see LN 1.16).

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: the fold of a garment forming a type of pocket or container

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a part of the sea which is partially enclosed by land
s.c: A ‘bay’ may be described as ‘a protected area of the sea’ or ‘a part of the sea protected by land.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: Abraham’s bosom) the heavenly abode, with the implication of close interpersonal relations
s.c: A literal rendering of κόλπος Ἀβραάμ as ‘the bosom of Abraham’ or ‘the lap of Abraham’ is often misleading. In some languages it may even suggest homosexuality, and in other cases it implies that Lazarus was either a baby or was changed into a baby in heaven. Since κόλπος Ἀβραάμ is generally interpreted as a reference to the eschatological heavenly feast, one may be justified in rendering ⟦Luke 16:22|Luke 16:22⟧ as in TEV ‘the poor man died and was carried by the angels to sit beside Abraham at the feast in heaven.’ In some languages κόλπος Ἀβραάμ in this context is translated as ‘he was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side’ or ‘… to be with Abraham.’

s.d: movement through water by the use of limbs
s.c: A number of languages have several different terms for ‘swim’ depending on whether it is a person, an animal, a fish, or an eel (or a snake). Care must be exercised in choosing the appropriate term for this context.

s.d: a relatively large construction for collecting water
s.c: The term κολυμβήθρα occurs in the NT only in ⟦John 5:2|John 5:2⟧, and refers to a pool having five porches, one on each of four sides and another porch which went across the middle of the pool

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Population Centers
s.d: a city or town with special privileges in that the inhabitants of such a town were regarded as Roman citizens (such towns were originally colonized by citizens of Rome)
s.c: A translational equivalent of ‘colony’ is frequently a phrase, for example, ‘a city where people were Romans’ or ‘a city of people who regarded Rome as their hometown.’

s.d: to wear long hair as part of one’s attire
s.g: to have long hair; to appear with long hair; to wear long hair
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate κομάω as ‘to let one’s hair grow long’ or ‘not to cut one’s hair.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: hair of the head of human beings
to carry or bring something to someone, usually implying a transfer
to cause someone to experience something on the basis of what that person has already done
s.g: to cause to experience in return; to cause to suffer for; to cause to experience in proportion to; to be repaid for

s.d: to receive as a type of compensation
to receive back something which one has previously possessed or its equivalent
s.g: to get back; to receive back; to be paid back

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: the state of being in better health after a previous state of relative lack of health
s.g: to be better; to be in better health

s.d: to apply whitewash to a surface
s.c: For many languages the closest equivalent of the phrase ‘whitewashed tombs’ is simply ‘tombs that have been painted white.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: (an idiom, literally: whitewashed wall) one who pretends to be one thing, while in reality he is something quite different

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: dust, soil (see also {D:2.16})
s.c: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

s.d: to cease, in reference to some type of movement
s.c: Languages may differ considerably in expressions relating to the ceasing of wind, for example, ‘the wind died,’ ‘the wind stood still,’ ‘the wind refused to move,’ or ‘the wind could not be felt.’

s.d: beating the breast and lamenting as an expression of sorrow{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

s.d: a violent and extensive slaughter, especially associated with armed conflicts
s.g: to kill; to slaughter; to defeat

s.d: to engage in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
s.g: hard work; toil; to work hard; to toil; to labor

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Tire, Rest
s.d: to be tired or weary, as the result of hard or difficult endeavor
s.g: to be tired; to be weary
s.c: It is also possible to interpret κοπιάω in ⟦Matthew 11:28|Matthew 11:28⟧ as κοπιάω ‘to work hard’ (see LN 42.47).

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοπιάω<SDBG:κοπιάω:000001>}[b] ‘to be tired,’ {D:23.78}) to become emotionally fatigued and discouraged
s.g: to give up; to lose heart

s.d: act of engaging in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: a state characterized by troubling circumstances

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Physiological Products of the Body
s.d: (derivative of {L:κόπριον<SDBG:κόπριον:000000>} ‘manure,’ {D:8.76}) a pile or heap of manure

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Physiological Products of the Body
s.d: fecal matter used as agricultural fertilizer
to cut, by means of a sharp-edged instrument (for example, knife, sword, or ax)
s.c: In a number of languages important distinctions are made for various types of cutting. For example, terms referring to the cutting of flesh may be different from those involving wood or stone. Similarly, important distinctions may be made as to whether there is simply an incision by cutting or whether a particular object is cut in two or cut off.

s.d: to beat the breast and lament as an expression of sorrow{N:001}
s.g: to mourn; to lament; to beat the breast; mourning; lamentation
s.c: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

s.d: large black bird with thick strong beak, and fairly short legs; highly intelligent; Corvus family; crows and ravens belong to the same family of birds but differ in size, ravens being somewhat larger and being more inclined to feed on dead bodies
s.c: In some languages one must be especially sensitive to connotations relating to terms for ‘crow’ or ‘raven,’ since these birds may be either particularly disliked or may be regarded as symbols of death and sickness. If such is the case, it may be preferable to simply use a more generic term for birds.

s.d: (a diminutive derivative of κόρη ‘girl,’ not occurring in the NT, but seemingly having lost the diminutive feature of meaning) a girl about the age of puberty
s.c: In ⟦Mark 5:41|Mark 5:41⟧ κοράσιον is equated in meaning with the Aramaic term ταλιθα (see LN 9.48), and in ⟦Mark 5:42|Mark 5:42⟧ this girl is identified as being twelve years of age. Compare also ἠνέχθη ἡ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πίνακι καὶ ἐδόθη τῷ κορασίῳ ‘his head was brought in on a plate and given to the girl’ (⟦Matthew 14:11|Matthew 14:11⟧). It is impossible to determine the age of Herodias’ daughter, but in view of her role as an attractive dancer, she was probably of the age of puberty.

s.d: (a borrowing from Hebrew) that which has been set aside as a gift to be given later to God, but which is still at the disposal of the owner
s.c: In some languages it is important to translate ‘corban’ as ‘what I have promised to later give to God.’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room in the Temple used as a treasury

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the leader of a rebellion against Moses
to be happy or content with what one has, with the implication of its being abundant
s.g: to be content; to be satisfied
s.c: Note that in this statement in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:8|1 Corinthians 4:8⟧ there is evidently a significant element of irony, and it is for that reason that some translations employ a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ For another interpretation of κορέννυμι in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:8|1 Corinthians 4:8⟧, see LN 57.22.

s.d: to have enough, often with the implication of even more than enough
s.g: to have enough; to be satiated
s.c: This first statement in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:8|1 Corinthians 4:8⟧ is probably to be understood ironically, and therefore it may be readily translated as a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ or as a statement referring to what the people of Corinth evidently presumed, for example, ‘you think you already have all you need.’ For another interpretation of κορέννυμι in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:8|1 Corinthians 4:8⟧, see LN 25.80.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Κόρινθος<SDBG:Κόρινθος:000000>} ‘Corinth,’ {D:93.506}) a person who lives in or is a native of Corinth

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Greece

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Roman centurion to whom Peter ministered

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Volume
s.d: a Hebrew dry measure for grain, flour, etc., of between ten and twelve bushels or about 390 liters
to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
s.g: to beautify; to adorn; to decorate; adornment; adorning

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: pertaining to the earth

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: (derivative of {L:κόσμος<SDBG:κόσμος:000002>}[c] ‘world system,’ {D:41.38}) pertaining to the system or standards of the world
s.c: In ⟦Titus 2:12|Titus 2:12⟧ τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας may also be rendered as ‘the desires which people in this world have,’ but in this context the term ἐπιθυμίας should imply wrong desires.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Modesty, Propriety
s.d: pertaining to being modest in the sense of moderate and wellordered
s.c: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in ⟦1 Timothy 2:9|1 Timothy 2:9⟧, see LN 66.10.

s.d: pertaining to being proper or suitable in terms of being attractive
s.c: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in ⟦1 Timothy 2:9|1 Timothy 2:9⟧, see LN 88.48.

s.d: one who rules over the whole world
s.c: The expression ‘world ruler’ should not be understood in terms of merely ruling over the earth as a physical object but of ‘ruling over those who are on the earth.’ Most scholars, however, interpret κοσμοκράτωρ in ⟦Ephesians 6:12|Ephesians 6:12⟧ as meaning a supernatural power (see LN 12.44), though it is possible to understand κοσμοκράτωρ in this context as meaning a human ruler.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
s.g: power; authority; lordship; ruler; wicked force
s.c: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of ⟦Ephesians 1:21|Ephesians 1:21⟧ some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Universe, Creation
s.d: the universe as an ordered structure
s.c: In many languages there is no specific term for the universe. The closest equivalent may simply be ‘all that exists.’ In other instances one may use a phrase such as ‘the world and all that is above it’ or ‘the sky and the earth.’ The concept of the totality of the universe may be expressed in some languages only as ‘everything that is on the earth and in the sky.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below{N:001}

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: the way humans typically conduct themselves in the world; the way things typically happen in human society
s.g: world system; the world’s standards; world
s.c: It may be particularly difficult to speak of the world being crucified (⟦Galatians 6:14|Galatians 6:14⟧), and therefore in a number of languages one must employ a somewhat fuller restructuring, for example, ‘because of Christ, the way in which people in this world live is as though it were dead as far as I am concerned, and I am dead, so to speak, as far as the way in which people in this world live.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κόσμος<SDBG:κόσμος:000000>}[a] ‘cosmos, universe,’ {D:1.1}) people associated with a world system and estranged from God
to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
s.g: to beautify; to adorn; to decorate; adornment; adorning
s.c: For another interpretation of κόσμος in ⟦1 Peter 3:3|1 Peter 3:3⟧, see LN 6.188.

s.d: an object which serves to adorn or beautify{N:003}
s.c: Adornments may be described as ‘things to make one look beautiful’ or ‘things with which one tries to appear attractive.’ For another interpretation of κόσμος in ⟦1 Peter 3:3|1 Peter 3:3⟧, see LN 79.12.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κόσμος<SDBG:κόσμος:000000>}[a] ‘world, universe,’ {D:1.1}) a great sum of something, implying an almost incredible totality
s.g: a world of; a tremendous amount of
s.c: In some languages the phrase ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας may be rendered as ‘the very symbol of evil,’ ‘a sign of what is truly evil,’ or ‘what is completely evil.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: title for supernatural forces and powers: a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
s.g: power; authority; lordship; ruler; wicked force
s.c: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. For example, ⟦Ephesians 2:2|Ephesians 2:2⟧ is rendered in some languages as ‘at that time you lived in the way in which the spirit that governs this world dictated you should live. This is the way the one who rules over the power in space commanded you to live. This is the very spirit that now commands the people who disobey God.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian who sent greetings in {S:04501602300038}

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Stand
s.d: (an Aramaic expression) to stand up from a reclining position
s.c: Note that κουμ is translated in ⟦Mark 5:41|Mark 5:41⟧ by ἐγείρω (see LN 17.9).

s.d: a group of soldiers serving as a guard
to cause something to weigh less
s.g: to lighten; to make less heavy

s.d: a relatively large basket used primarily for food or produce{N:001}
s.c: Translators often find it difficult to obtain satisfactory equivalents of σπυρίς (LN 6.149) and κόφινος, since in various receptor languages there are highly specific terms for particular kinds of baskets depending upon type of construction and size. Unfortunately, there is no way of determining from the Greek text precisely the size or type of baskets involved in references to σπυρίς and κόφινος.

s.d: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
s.c: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

s.d: to shout or cry out, with the possible implication of the unpleasant nature of the sound{N:001}

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Drunkenness
s.d: drunken behavior which is completely without moral restraint
s.c: In a number of languages it may be possible to translate κραιπάλη as ‘bad things people do when they are very drunk.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the bony framework of the head, especially the upper portion
s.g: skull (in the NT κρανίον is used only as a name for the hill of Golgotha)
s.c: In rendering κρανίου τόπος ‘place of the skull’ it may be necessary to indicate clearly the relationship between place and skull. A literal rendering of such a phrase might simply mean ‘a place where there was a skull.’ However the meaning of Golgotha has been interpreted generally as ‘a hill resembling a skull’ and therefore κρανίου τόπος may be more satisfactorily rendered as ‘a place resembling a skull’ or ‘a hill looking like a skull.’ See LN 93.453.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: decorative tassel attached to the bottom edge of a long outer garment{N:001}
s.c: The edge of the garment designated by κράσπεδον could have been plain or decorated. In ⟦Matthew 23:5|Matthew 23:5⟧ κράσπεδον denotes the tassels worn at the four corners of the outer garment (see LN 6.194). It is also possible that in all instances in which κράσπεδον is used in reference to Jesus’ clothing, the reference may be specifically to the tassels and not merely to the fringe or edge of the garment. The interpretation of such passages depends upon how strictly Jesus may have followed the Mosaic law and the manner in which the authors may have understood the meaning of κράσπεδον.

s.d: the tassels which Jews were obliged to wear on the four corners of the outer garment (see {S:00401503700000-00401504100000})
s.c: In some languages tassels may be described as ‘decorated corners’ or ‘ribbons at the corners.’ See the discussion at LN 6.180.
